title: A Study in Scarlet
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
summary: O doutor Watson volta ferido da guerra no Afeganistão e vai dividir um apartamento em Londres com um homem muito estranho, Sherlock Holmes. Logo os dois são chamados para ver um morto numa casa vazia, com a palavra RACHE escrita em sangue na parede. Para resolver o mistério, Holmes vai usar sua ciência da dedução, e a resposta está numa velha história de amor e vingança nos desertos da América.

chapters.title: Mr Sherlock Holmes
paragraphs: In the year 1878 I became a doctor, and soon after that I went to the war in Afghanistan. It was a terrible time for me. A bullet hit me in the shoulder, and later I became very ill with fever. The army sent me back to England, thin and weak, with very little money.
I lived in a small hotel in London, but it was too expensive. One day I was in a bar when someone touched my arm. It was young Stamford, an old friend from my hospital days.
“Watson!” he said. “You're as thin as a stick and as brown as a nut. What happened to you?”
I told him my story over lunch. “Now I need cheap rooms,” I said. “But I can't pay for them alone.”
Stamford looked at me strangely. “You're the second man today to say that,” he said. “There's a man at the hospital who wants to share some nice rooms. His name is Sherlock Holmes.”
“Is he a doctor?” I asked.

“No. Nobody really knows what he does. He studies chemistry and many other strange things. Once I saw him hit dead bodies with a stick, because he wanted to see if they could get bruises after death.”
“Then let's go and meet him,” I said.
We found Holmes alone in the chemistry laboratory. He was tall and thin, with a sharp nose and quick, clever eyes. When he saw us, he ran towards us with a test tube in his hand.
“I've found it! I've found it!” he cried. “A new test for blood. It works even with very old stains. Now the police can catch many more criminals.”
Then he shook my hand. “How are you?” he said. “You have been in Afghanistan, I see.”
“How on earth did you know that?” I asked in surprise.

Holmes only smiled. We talked about the rooms. He told me he sometimes played the violin and sometimes did not speak for days. I told him I was lazy and did not like noise. The next day we looked at the rooms at 221B Baker Street, and we took them at once.

chapters.title: The Science of Deduction
paragraphs: My new friend was a mystery to me. Some days he worked all day in the laboratory. On other days he lay on the sofa and did not say a word. He knew a lot about chemistry, poisons, mud and crime, but he knew nothing about books, history or the stars. He did not even know that the Earth goes round the Sun.
“Why should I care?” he said when I told him. “It doesn't help me in my work.”

Many strange visitors came to our rooms. There was a small man with a face like a rat, called Lestrade. There was a young girl, an old man, and a railway porter. Every time, Holmes asked me to leave the sitting room.
One morning I read an article in a magazine. It said that a clever person can understand everything about a stranger from his hands, his clothes and his face.
“What nonsense!” I said. “This writer lives in a dream.”
“I wrote it,” said Holmes calmly. “And it's not a dream. It's my work. I'm a consulting detective. When the police have a problem, they come to me. That's how I knew you were in Afghanistan.”
“Please explain,” I said.

“It was easy. You looked like a doctor, but you had the manner of a soldier. So, an army doctor. Your face was brown, but your wrists were white, so you came from a hot country. Your face was tired and thin, so you were ill. You held your left arm stiffly, so it was hurt. Where can an English army doctor get a brown face and a bad arm? In Afghanistan, of course.”
Just then a man in uniform knocked at the door with a letter. Holmes read it and passed it to me. It was from Tobias Gregson of Scotland Yard.
“There has been a bad business at number 3, Lauriston Gardens,” it said. “A man is dead in an empty house. There is blood, but no wound. Please come.”
“Gregson and Lestrade are the best of a bad lot,” said Holmes, and he put on his coat. “Come with me, Watson. This may be interesting.”

chapters.title: The House in Lauriston Gardens
paragraphs: Number 3 was an ugly, empty house with dirty windows. A small garden of wet clay was in front of it. Holmes did not go in at once. He walked slowly along the path and looked carefully at the ground.
Gregson and Lestrade met us at the door. “We've touched nothing,” said Gregson proudly.

In the dining room lay the body of a man about forty years old. He was well dressed, but his face was terrible. It was full of fear and hate. There was no wound on him, but there was blood on the floor.
“His name is Enoch Drebber, from Cleveland, in America,” said Gregson. “We found cards in his pocket, and a gold watch and money. Nobody robbed him.”
Holmes knelt and smelled the dead man's lips. Then the policemen lifted the body, and something fell on the floor. It was a woman's wedding ring.
“This makes it more difficult,” said Lestrade. But then he cried out, “Look at this!” On the wall, in red blood, someone had written one word: RACHE.
“The murderer wanted to write the name Rachel,” said Lestrade, “but he didn't finish. Find Rachel and you'll find the killer.”
Holmes laughed. “Rache is a German word,” he said. “It means revenge. But don't believe it. Somebody wants us to look for a German.”
Then he looked at the floor and the walls with a magnifying glass. He measured things with a tape and picked up some grey ash.

“I can tell you a few things,” he said at last. “The murderer was a tall man, over six feet. He was young and had a red face. His boots were square and he smoked a Trichinopoly cigar. He came here with the dead man in a cab. And the dead man was poisoned.”
The two policemen stared at him. Then Holmes and I went to see John Rance, the constable who found the body. Rance told us that in the night he saw a drunk man at the garden gate, singing loudly.
“A drunk man!” cried Holmes angrily. “That was the murderer, you fool! He came back for the ring, and you let him go.”

chapters.title: The Old Woman and the Second Death
paragraphs: “The man will come back for the ring,” said Holmes that evening. “It's very important to him. So I'm going to use it as bait.” He put an advertisement in all the newspapers: Found, a gold wedding ring, in the street near Lauriston Gardens. Ask for Dr Watson, 221B Baker Street.
“And if the murderer comes?” I asked.
“Then you'll need your old army gun,” he answered.

At eight o'clock the bell rang. But it was not a tall man. It was a very old woman with a wrinkled face. “It's my daughter Sally's ring,” she said in a weak voice. “She lost it at the circus last night.” I gave her the ring, and she went slowly down the stairs.

Holmes put on his coat and followed her. He came home very late, laughing at himself. “She got into a cab,” he said, “and I ran behind it. But when it stopped, the cab was empty! That old woman was a young man, and a very good actor. He jumped out while the cab was moving. He has friends who help him, Watson.”

Two days later, Lestrade came to our rooms. His face was pale. “Drebber had a secretary, Joseph Stangerson,” he said. “I found him this morning at Halliday's Private Hotel. Somebody stabbed him in the heart. And on the wall, written in blood, was the word RACHE.”
“Did you find anything in his room?” asked Holmes quickly.
“Only some money, a novel, and a small box with two pills in it.”
“Give me those pills,” said Holmes. His eyes were shining.

Our landlady had an old dog. It was very ill, and she wanted to end its pain. Holmes cut one pill in half and gave it to the dog in some milk. Nothing happened. He waited, and his face became worried. Then he took the second pill and gave half to the dog. The poor animal shook and died at once.
“I knew it!” cried Holmes. “One pill was harmless, and one was poison. Now everything is clear.”

chapters.title: The Cabman
paragraphs: Gregson came to our rooms, very excited. “I've got the murderer!” he said. “He's a young navy officer called Arthur Charpentier. Drebber stayed at his mother's house and was rude to his sister.”
Lestrade arrived with the news about Stangerson. Gregson's face fell. His prisoner was in prison when Stangerson died.
“Gentlemen,” said Holmes, “I know the name of the murderer.”
Just then six or seven dirty little boys ran into the room. They were the Baker Street Irregulars, Holmes's street boys. They could go everywhere and hear everything.
“Wiggins,” said Holmes to their leader, “bring a cab here.” A few minutes later the boy came back. “The cab's downstairs, sir,” he said.
“Please ask the cabman to come up and help me with my box,” said Holmes. He was kneeling by a small travelling box.
The cabman came in. He was a big, strong man with a red face. He bent down to help with the box. Then there was a sharp click, and Holmes jumped up.
“Gentlemen,” he said, “let me introduce Mr Jefferson Hope, the murderer of Enoch Drebber and Joseph Stangerson.”

There were handcuffs on the cabman's wrists. For a moment he did not move. Then he fought like a wild animal. He threw us about the room and almost broke the window. It took all four of us to hold him down.
“How did you find him?” asked Gregson when Hope was quiet.

“I sent a telegram to the police in Cleveland,” said Holmes. “They told me that Drebber was afraid of an old enemy called Jefferson Hope. The murderer was tall, came in a cab, and could follow Drebber everywhere. So he was a cabman. My boys looked at every cab in London until they found him.”

Hope looked at us calmly. “I'm not going to fight anymore,” he said. “I have a disease of the heart. I haven't got long to live, so I want to tell you my story. But first you must hear what happened twenty years ago, far away in the deserts of America.”

chapters.title: The Flower of Utah
paragraphs: In 1847, in the great desert of North America, a man was dying of thirst. His name was John Ferrier. With him was a little girl of five called Lucy. Her parents were dead, and the other travellers were dead too.
“Are we going to die?” asked Lucy.
“I'm afraid so, my dear,” said Ferrier, and they fell asleep on a rock.

But they did not die. A long line of wagons came across the desert. They were the Mormons, a religious group, and their leader was Brigham Young. “We will save you,” he said, “but you must live with us and follow our religion.” Ferrier agreed.
The Mormons built a city in Utah, and Ferrier became a rich farmer. Lucy grew up and became the most beautiful girl in the country. People called her the Flower of Utah.

One day her horse was in danger in the middle of a group of cows. A young hunter rode into the cows and saved her. His name was Jefferson Hope. He was not a Mormon. He came often to the farm after that, and soon he and Lucy were in love.
“I must go to the mountains for two months to look for silver,” he told her. “When I come back, I'll marry you.”
But Brigham Young visited Ferrier. “Your daughter must marry a Mormon,” he said. “Drebber and Stangerson both have sons. She must choose one of them. You have thirty days.”

Every morning after that, Ferrier found a number on his house: 29, 28, 27. It was a terrible warning. On the last night, Jefferson Hope came back. In the dark, the three of them escaped into the mountains.
One day Hope went to hunt for food. When he came back, Ferrier and Lucy were gone. There was only a grave with these words: John Ferrier, died August 4th, 1860.

Lucy had to marry young Enoch Drebber. A month later, she died of a broken heart. On the night before her funeral, Hope came into the room, kissed her cold face and took the wedding ring from her finger. “She won't be buried with that,” he said, and he ran into the night.

chapters.title: Jefferson Hope's Story
paragraphs: “After that I lived only for revenge,” said Hope. “Drebber and Stangerson left Utah because they were afraid of me. I followed them for years, across America and then to Europe. I had no money, so I worked. In London I became a cabman.
“One night Drebber was drunk, and he got into my cab. I took him to the empty house in Lauriston Gardens. There I showed him Lucy's ring. ‘Do you remember her?’ I said. His face became white.

“I didn't want to kill him like a criminal. I had a box with two pills, one with poison and one without. ‘Choose one,’ I said. ‘I'll take the other. Let God decide.’ He took one, and I swallowed the other. A minute later he fell dead. My nose bled because I was so excited, and I wrote RACHE on the wall with my blood. Then I noticed I had lost the ring, so I went back for it. The policeman thought I was drunk.
“I waited for Stangerson outside his hotel. When I gave him the choice, he jumped at my throat. So I had to use my knife. And that's all, gentlemen. My work is done.”
We were all silent. The story was so sad that even Lestrade had nothing to say.
But Jefferson Hope never stood before a judge. That night, his sick heart broke, and he died in his prison cell. There was a peaceful smile on his face.
The next day Holmes laughed as he showed me the newspaper. It said that the clever Gregson and Lestrade had caught the murderer. Holmes's name was there only as a friend who helped them a little.
“You see, Watson?” he said. “In this world it doesn't matter what you do. It only matters what people believe you did.”

“Never mind,” I said. “I've written everything in my notebook. One day the world will know the true story.” I decided to call it A Study in Scarlet, because there is a scarlet thread of murder in the colourless thread of life, and our job is to find it.
